fatal_errors: The proposed intervention omits the governing intervention in the target study: atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L followed by annealing, especially at 550 °C.
The short-range-order evidence concerns CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys and mechanical slip behavior, not corrosion resistance of chromium-bearing steels or passive-film templating.

The proposed heat-treatment comparison does not control for grain size, residual stress, precipitation, and phase changes, so it cannot uniquely attribute corrosion differences to short-range ordering.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses corrosion-resistant alloys and makes testable predictions involving passive films, lower corrosion current, and reduced material loss. It is therefore a scientifically plausible alternative rather than wholly unsupported. However, it reconstructs little of the target study: it replaces an AlCoCrFeNi plasma-sprayed coating on SS316L with hypothetical Cr-rich nanoclusters in bulk steel, omits the coating architecture and 550 °C optimum, and uses NaCl testing rather than 3.5 wt% H2SO4 and cyclic 900 °C Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 exposure. The only substantial mechanistic overlap is chromium-rich passivation. The baseline uses identical composition, which is useful, but different heat treatments can alter numerous microstructural variables besides ordering. TEM confirmation, polarization, and passive-film analysis could reveal a correlation, yet stronger causal discrimination would require matched grain size, phases, residual stress, and Cr depletion, plus direct nanoscale ordering measurements before and after exposure. E1 and E2 support general corrosion resistance of multicomponent-alloy coatings, while E3 establishes short-range ordering and mechanical effects in CrCoNi; none directly supports the claimed ordering-to-passivation mechanism.
